lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you met biomes. Which biome holds more than half of all kinds of land plants and animals? (The tropical rainforest.) Today: how climate, soil and living things are linked.

An ecosystem is living things and their surroundings working together: plants, animals and tiny decomposers (the biotic parts), with the climate, soil, water and rocks (the abiotic parts). A biome is a very large ecosystem, such as the tundra.

Climate decides the biome. Near the Equator it is hot and wet all year, about 27 °C with rain on most days: tropical rainforest. Deserts get under 250 mm of rain a year; the tundra is cold, with frozen ground below.

Energy flows through an ecosystem. Plants, the producers, capture sunlight. Plant-eaters get only about a tenth of the plants' energy, and meat-eaters about a tenth of theirs; the rest is used up living. So there are far fewer foxes than rabbits.

Nutrients cycle between three stores: living things (biomass), fallen leaves (litter) and the soil. In a rainforest, heat and rain rot leaves in weeks, and plants take the nutrients up fast. So most are in the plants, and the soil is thin.

In the cold taiga, fallen needles rot very slowly, so a thick layer of litter builds up. Much of the nutrients wait there. Each biome's plants and animals suit its climate and soil: change one part, and the others change too.

People change ecosystems: forests are cut for cattle, crops and wood, and thin rainforest soil soon washes away. Sustainable choices help: protected areas, replanting, and farming that keeps the trees, such as cacao and coffee grown in the forest's shade.
Try it in the world: build two small biomes side by side, a rainforest and a taiga, with the right plants. Put a sign in each showing where most of its nutrients are stored. Next: water supply.

exercises.prompt: What are plants called in an ecosystem, because they make food from sunlight?
exercises.hint: They produce food for everything else.
exercises.explain: Producers: plants make their own food from sunlight, and every other living thing depends on it.

exercises.prompt: Which is an abiotic (non-living) part of an ecosystem?
exercises.explain: Rainfall; trees, beetles and mushrooms are living (biotic).

exercises.prompt: Deserts get under 250 mm of rain a year.

exercises.hint: Look at the temperature line and the rain bars.
exercises.explain: Hot all year and wet every month: tropical rainforest.

exercises.hint: Think of worms, fungi and bacteria.
choices: break down dead things and return nutrients
exercises.explain: They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil.

exercises.prompt: Grass stores 20,000 units of energy, and about a tenth passes to the rabbits that eat it. How many units reach the rabbits?
In which store are most of this rainforest's nutrients?
exercises.hint: The biggest circle holds the most.
exercises.explain: In the biomass: plants take nutrients up almost as soon as leaves rot.

exercises.prompt: Why is rainforest soil thin and poor?
exercises.hint: What happens to fallen leaves in the heat and rain?
choices: plants take the nutrients up fast
exercises.explain: Leaves rot fast and plants take the nutrients up at once, and heavy rain washes the rest away.

exercises.prompt: Match each biome to its feature.
exercises.hint: Two are cold, two are hot.
exercises.explain: Tundra: permafrost. Savanna: grass, wet and dry seasons. Taiga: conifers. Hot desert: very little rain.

exercises.prompt: Sort these parts of an ecosystem: living or non-living?
exercises.hint: Is it, or was it ever, alive?
exercises.explain: Living: trees, worms, fungi. Non-living: sunlight, rain, rocks.

exercises.prompt: An owl gets 30 units of energy from mice, which ate plants. About how many units were in the plants?
exercises.hint: Two steps down: multiply by 10 twice.

exercises.prompt: Why does litter pile up in the taiga?
exercises.hint: Decomposers work faster when it is warm.
choices: the cold makes fallen needles rot slowly
exercises.explain: Cold slows decomposers, so needles rot slowly and a thick litter layer builds up.

exercises.prompt: Changing one part of an ecosystem never affects the others.
exercises.hint: Think of cutting the rainforest's trees.
exercises.explain: False: the parts are linked; cut the trees and the thin soil washes away.

exercises.prompt: Which is a sustainable way to farm in a rainforest?
exercises.hint: Which one keeps the forest standing?
choices: grow cacao in the shade of the trees
cut all the trees for cattle
plant one crop on bare soil
exercises.explain: Growing cacao or coffee in the forest's shade keeps the trees, the soil and the wildlife.

exercises.prompt: Put this food chain in order, from where its energy starts.
exercises.hint: Energy starts with the Sun and passes to what eats what.
